title: The Small Tide
premise: Marguerite Quintana keeps her late grandfather's lighthouse on the Cornish coast and her heart locked just as tightly, writing novels under a pseudonym no one can trace. When a storm washes up a mailbag containing a letter postmarked eleven years ago—written by her grandfather to a woman Marguerite never knew existed—she begins investigating the secret life of the man who taught her that love is a discipline of distance. Her search draws in Elias Wrenn, a terminally ill archivist passing through on the last coastal train line before it closes forever, whose own unfinished letters mirror hers. As the lighthouse's decommission date approaches, Marguerite must choose between the safety of invisibility and letting Elias stay past the final departure; she learns her grandfather's letter was never sent because he chose to stay for family, not run from love. In the end, Marguerite sends both letters—the old one and her own—and keeps the light burning as a home rather than a warning.
about_author: Gideon Ravensworth is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered correspondence from decommissioned British lighthouses. They write slow-burn romances about people who mistake solitude for safety, and live within earshot of the sea they refuse to romanticize.

chapters.title: The Muscle of the Heart
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She tends the lighthouse, teaches herself emotional containment like calisthenics, and finishes another novel under her pseudonym. A routine inventory reveals her grandfather's meticulous logs end abruptly eleven years ago. Beat: establish her philosophy of controlled distance and its quiet cost.

chapters.title: What the Storm Returns
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. After a gale, wreckage including an old postal sack washes into the cove; inside is a water-stained letter addressed to 'V.' at a demolished seaside hotel, signed by her grandfather, postmarked the month his logs stopped. Beat: the crack in the wall of her certainty.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Introduce Elias Wrenn, an archivist cataloguing the closure of the coastal railway, hiding his diagnosis behind professional efficiency. He arrives in town to document the line's final season and notices the lighthouse still manned against regulation. Beat: two keepers of dying systems meet.

chapters.title: Questions Asked Sideways
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She questions the postmistress, Mrs. Calloway, who goes pale at the name V. and warns her some letters stay lost on purpose. Marguerite lies to Elias about why she's asking around. Beat: guilt of the investigator; first lie between them.

chapters.title: A Room at the Harbourside
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Lodgings fall through; Marguerite grudgingly rents him her grandfather's old boathouse. Their proximity forces small negotiations—shared kettles, borrowed books—that unsettle her routines. Beat: found-family seed planted; resistance to it.

chapters.title: The Hotel That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She finds the Avalon Hotel was demolished nine years ago; its owner, Vivienne Marsh, moved inland. A photograph shows her grandfather and Vivienne laughing on the gallery deck. Beat: the grandfather becomes a stranger; grief complicates the mystery.

chapters.title: Manuscript in the Wall
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Repairing boathouse plaster, Elias uncovers a manuscript draft—Marguerite's unpublished novel, unmistakably autobiographical, about a girl raised by a man afraid of being left. He says nothing. Beat: intimacy through secrecy; his tenderness deepens.

chapters.title: Vivienne Marsh Receives No One
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She travels inland; Vivienne, now elderly, slams the door—but slips a note under it: 'Ask him why he never posted it. Then ask yourself.' Beat: the mystery turns inward; Marguerite suspects her own role in the silence.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Weather
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Flashback fragments surface: young Marguerite's feverish winter, her parents' deaths, the grandfather's cancelled trips. Present-day Marguerite realizes the unsent letter coincides with the year she nearly died. Beat: devastating hypothesis—she was the reason.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Box
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. His symptoms worsen; he catalogs his own life into boxes for whoever comes after. He almost tells Marguerite, instead asks what she'd do with time if she knew its length. Beat: rising tension; love declared obliquely.

chapters.title: Decommission Notice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Official word: the lighthouse will be automated and the cottage sold at season's end—the same week the last train runs. Everything she anchors herself to has an expiry date. Beat: external stakes crystallize; panic masquerading as planning.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud in the Dark
chapters.summary: Both POVs. During a blackout, Marguerite reads her published novel aloud by lamplight, revealing her pseudonym to Elias without saying so; he pretends not to know, then confesses he found the manuscript. First real fight, first real honesty. Beat: walls tested and cracked.

chapters.title: Mrs. Calloway's Confession
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The postmistress admits she kept the letter back at the grandfather's request—he asked her to hold it 'until I'm brave,' and he never came back for it. She gives Marguerite a second envelope, unopened, addressed to Marguerite herself. Beat: midpoint revelation; the past hands her a choice.

chapters.title: The Letter to Me
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She reads her grandfather's words: he loved Vivienne, but chose the child who needed him; he hoped Marguerite would learn love is staying, not sacrifice. She rages—she never asked him to give up his life. Beat: anger as grief; theme inverted.

chapters.title: Vivienne's Door Opens
chapters.summary: Elias accompanies Marguerite inland. Vivienne, softened by Elias's visible frailty, shares her side: she waited two years, then built a life; she doesn't regret it, but she kept every tide table he ever sent. Beat: forgiveness modeled; survival's price acknowledged without bitterness.

chapters.title: What Elias Packed
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He receives scan results; treatment might buy a year, maybe less. He drafts a departure, telling himself leaving spares her the ending. Marguerite finds the packed bag and the medical file together. Beat: crisis of trust; her oldest fear confirmed.

chapters.title: You Don't Get to Decide My Grief
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Confrontation in the lantern room during a rising storm. She names the pattern: everyone leaves protectively, deciding for her. Elias argues mercy; she argues agency. He stays the night anyway, on the floor, neither yielding. Beat: climax of emotional conflict.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The railway's final day; the town gathers on the platform. Elias stands at the door of the carriage. Marguerite arrives late, breathless, and instead of asking him to stay, she boards with him—one stop, together, then back. Beat: climax resolved through action, not persuasion.

chapters.title: Staying Is a Verb
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He moves his boxes out of storage and into the cottage; they negotiate illness honestly—appointments, bad days, the shape of a year. Marguerite writes for the first time as herself, not the pseudonym. Beat: falling action; love as daily practice.

chapters.title: Posting the Letter
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She mails her grandfather's letter to Vivienne with a note of explanation, and posts her own new letter—to the future keeper of the lighthouse—into the old lamp room's maintenance hatch, a tradition she invents. Beat: memory honored; cycles broken.

chapters.title: The Light Kept Burning
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Decommission day: the automated system takes over, but the couple remains as caretakers of the cottage and archive. Elias's health holds, uncertainly; they stop counting in years and start counting in tides. Beat: quiet resolution; found family grows—a visiting niece, Mrs. Calloway at Sunday supper.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Postmarked Tomorrow
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, one year later. Her first novel under her own name publishes; its dedication reads 'For the ones who stayed.' A storm brings a new piece of sea-glass mail—an answer from a stranger who found her letter in the lamp room. Beat: hope renewed; the heart, trained at last, opens on purpose.
